title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text: A seed can remain dormant in apparently suitable soil. A shoot bends towards light, and a mature plant begins flowering after the season changes. Explain how perception, signalling, altered cellular activity and organ development connect. Distinguish a response from proof of its underlying mechanism.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text: A seed can remain dormant in apparently suitable soil. A shoot bends towards light, and a mature plant begins flowering after the season changes. Explain how perception, signalling, altered cellular activity and organ development connect. Distinguish a response from proof of its underlying mechanism.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
From stimulus to response
A signal must be detected by an appropriate receptor. Detection changes downstream activity, which can modify existing proteins, transport, metabolism or gene expression. The response depends on tissue, developmental state and other signals. A receptor is not the final response itself, and the amount of a hormone is not the only determinant of sensitivity.
Gene expression connects a shared genome to specialised behaviour. Transcription produces RNA; some RNAs support protein synthesis and others act directly. Regulatory proteins can change which genes are used and when. Changing gene expression does not require changing DNA sequence. Fast ion-channel responses can precede slower changes in organ anatomy.





flowchart LR
  cue[Environmental or internal cue] --> receptor[Perception]
  receptor --> fast[Existing protein and transport activity]
  receptor --> expr[Gene-expression changes]
  fast --> cell[Cell physiology]
  expr --> cell
  cell --> organ[Growth or developmental response]
  state[Tissue and developmental state] --> cell






This original scheme is a reasoning framework. Actual pathways have feedback, interactions and distinct timescales. Use it to locate the evidence: does an experiment measure a stimulus, an intermediate or the final phenotype?

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Hormones operate in interacting networks
Plant hormones are signalling molecules active at low concentrations. Their effects depend on production, transport, metabolism and perception. One hormone can affect several processes, and several hormones can affect one process. The following are useful entry points rather than one-to-one rules:








Signal class
Useful example
Interpretation caution




Auxin
Directional growth, root initiation and developmental patterning
Concentration, transport and tissue sensitivity matter


Cytokinins
Cell division, meristem activity and resource-related responses
Effects interact with other signals and developmental state


Gibberellins
Germination and stem elongation in appropriate contexts
Not every dwarf plant lacks gibberellin


ABA
Dormancy and water-stress responses
ABA responses include both rapid physiology and longer-term development


Ethylene
Fruit ripening in responsive species and other developmental/stress responses
Not all fruits use identical ripening regulation


Brassinosteroids
Growth and differentiation
Effects depend on interaction with other pathways


Jasmonates and salicylic acid
Defence and associated growth changes
Different attackers and conditions recruit different combinations



Memorising this table is insufficient. Explain a case as signal → cellular process → organ consequence. For example, a change in auxin distribution can produce unequal expansion across an organ. Root and shoot growth responses to the same auxin change can differ. “Auxin promotes growth” hides this important context dependence.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: Light supplies information as well as energy
text:
Light supplies information as well as energy
Photoreceptors allow plants to detect spectral composition, direction and timing. Phytochromes respond to red/far-red light, while blue-light receptors include cryptochromes and phototropins. These signals influence developmental choices beyond photosynthetic energy supply. A seedling can change form after a small informative light exposure without obtaining much fixed carbon from it.
Red/far-red balance can provide information about neighbouring vegetation. A shoot may respond with altered elongation and resource allocation. This can improve access to light but can also increase vulnerability or reduce investment elsewhere. A response is conditional, not evidence that plants predict an intentional goal.
Phototropism involves directional light perception and differential growth. Gravitropism involves gravity perception, signal redistribution and asymmetric responses. Gravitational orientation and light direction are different cues; an experimental design must separate them before assigning a mechanism. Rotating a pot changes several physical relationships and requires controls.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: Germination depends on state and conditions
text:
Germination depends on state and conditions
Imbibition restores hydration, and metabolism resumes as conditions permit. Reserve mobilisation supports the developing seedling. Radicle emergence is a commonly used operational measure of germination, but later establishment requires further growth and resource acquisition.
Dormancy means a viable seed does not germinate despite otherwise suitable conditions. Quiescence reflects unsuitable external conditions such as insufficient water. Dormancy can involve embryo state, surrounding tissues and signal balance. ABA and gibberellin pathways provide a useful model of interacting regulation, but species differ in requirements for temperature, light or other cues.
A germination percentage needs a clear denominator and time. Twelve germinated seeds out of twenty by day five gives 60%, not proof that eight are dead. They could germinate later, be dormant, or be non-viable. Independent dishes or pots matter when environmental treatment is shared. Twenty seeds in one dish do not automatically give twenty independent temperature treatments.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: Vegetative growth combines production and allocation
text:
Vegetative growth combines production and allocation
Meristems generate organs while expansion changes their dimensions. Hormones, nutrients, carbon status and environment coordinate these processes. Apical dominance illustrates integration: shoot-tip activity influences lateral bud outgrowth through several interacting signals and resource relations. Removing an apex changes more than one hormone concentration and creates a wound. An altered branching pattern alone cannot identify the complete mechanism.
Secondary growth increases girth through lateral meristems. Cambial activity must be coordinated with transport and support as the shoot enlarges. Seasonal activity can alter xylem properties. A ring or tissue pattern records growth, but interpreting it requires knowledge of species and environmental history.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: Flowering connects leaves and the shoot apex
text:
Flowering connects leaves and the shoot apex
Plants integrate age, resource status, temperature and light timing. Photoperiod responses depend on the species and can involve the duration of the night as well as the day. Vernalisation refers to promotion of flowering competence by extended cold in responsive plants. It is different from a universal direct trigger that makes every cold-treated plant flower immediately.
In Arabidopsis, FT provides an example of a mobile signal linking leaves with the shoot apex. Experiments expressing tagged FT and using grafts supported protein movement contributing to floral induction. This is evidence for a particular mechanism in a model system, not proof that all flowering control is identical. See the primary study by Corbesier and colleagues.
At the apex, altered gene activity changes meristem identity and organ development. Flower induction, formation of floral organs, gametophyte development, pollination, fertilisation and fruit development are distinct steps. Failure at one step need not mean that flowering was not induced.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Reproduction links generations
In flowering plants, pollen delivers sperm cells to the female gametophyte. Double fertilisation produces a zygote and endosperm, with the latter supporting seed development in an appropriate species-specific pattern. Embryogenesis establishes the next plant’s body organisation. Fruit derives from maternal tissue and can assist protection and dispersal; a seed and a fruit are not equivalent structures.
Developing seeds and fruits draw resources as sinks. Carbon limitation, water stress or temperature can affect reproductive success after a normal-looking flower forms. Measure seed number, viability or yield separately from flower number when those are the actual biological goals.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Senescence can redistribute resources
Senescence is a regulated developmental process that can mobilise nutrients from ageing tissues. Programmed cell death participates in development and defence, but it should not be treated as synonymous with every senescence stage or every form of accidental injury. A yellowing leaf may reflect normal ageing, deficiency, stress or several processes. Tissue age and environmental controls are needed to distinguish explanations.
For an accessible introduction to light and hormone responses, consult OpenStax plant sensory systems. Work through the exercise and self-check before the final unit connects these signals to stress and applications.

section: 1. Must a signalling response involve new DNA sequence?
text:
1. Must a signalling response involve new DNA sequence?






Explanation





No. Existing protein activity and gene-expression changes can alter physiology without changing sequence.

title: P4 — Development self-check
section: 2. Does one hormone specify exactly one response?
text:
2. Does one hormone specify exactly one response?






Explanation





No. Effects depend on dose, tissue, development, sensitivity, transport and interactions with other pathways.

title: P4 — Development self-check
section: 3. How does dormancy differ from quiescence?
text:
3. How does dormancy differ from quiescence?






Explanation





A dormant viable seed fails to germinate despite otherwise suitable conditions; quiescence reflects unsuitable external conditions.

title: P4 — Development self-check
section: 4. What is 18 germinated seeds out of 24?
text:
4. What is 18 germinated seeds out of 24?






Explanation





75%, at the specified observation time. The remaining six are not necessarily dead.

title: P4 — Development self-check
text:
5. What does Arabidopsis FT illustrate?






Explanation





A mobile protein signal contributing to communication between leaves and the shoot apex during floral induction; gene expression and product movement are distinct.

title: P4 — Development self-check
section: 6. Do equal flower numbers establish equal reproductive success?
text:
6. Do equal flower numbers establish equal reproductive success?






Explanation





No. Pollination, fertilisation, seed development and viability can differ after flowers form.

title: P4 — Development self-check
section: 7. Is every yellow leaf proof of programmed senescence?
text:
7. Is every yellow leaf proof of programmed senescence?






Explanation





No. Deficiency, injury and other stress can produce yellowing. Time course, context and physiological evidence are needed.



Compare your reasoning with the exercise. Correct an explanation rather than recording only a score.

title: P1 exercise — Explain the structure
text: Work from the tutorial. Allow about 45–60 minutes, including discussion. These classroom descriptions are invented; they are not substitute microscope images or instructions for handling specimens. Leave with labelled drawings and short mechanistic explanations. No software is needed.

title: P1 exercise — Explain the structure
text:
1. Follow material through a leaf
Draw epidermis, a stomatal pore, an internal air space, mesophyll, xylem and phloem. Trace CO2, water and exported carbohydrate using separate labelled arrows. Mark where at least one membrane must be crossed. Explain why opening the pore can increase both carbon access and water loss. Do not draw phloem as an extension of the stomatal pore.






Start with compartments





CO2 reaches mesophyll from the atmosphere; water arrives through vascular tissue. A photosynthetic product’s eventual export is a different pathway. An arrow between organs is not a claim that no membranes lie along the route.

title: P1 exercise — Explain the structure
text:
2. Classify evidence, not just names
For each invented observation, identify a plausible cell/tissue function and one additional feature needed before a confident identification.







Description
Observation




A
An elongated conducting element lacks living contents and has thick lignified walls


B
A living photosynthetic cell borders a large internal air space


C
A living epidermal cell has a long extension into the surrounding soil


D
A population near a shoot tip contains small actively dividing cells



Why would “thick wall” alone fail to identify xylem? Why does a text exercise not demonstrate that you can recognise the tissue on an actual slide?

title: P1 exercise — Explain the structure
section: 3. Root growth has more than one explanation
text:
3. Root growth has more than one explanation
In this invented simplified model, a marked root segment contains 100 cells arranged end to end. Ignore gaps and assume the measured cell length represents the whole segment. Mean length is 40 µm before and 70 µm after a period with no divisions. Calculate segment length at both times in millimetres and its increase. Compare with a second case containing 175 cells of 40 µm each.






Check the scale





100 × 40 µm = 4000 µm = 4 mm; 100 × 70 µm = 7 mm. The increase is 3 mm. 175 × 40 µm is also 7 mm. Equal final lengths can arise through different cellular processes. Real tissue has heterogeneous cell lengths and geometry.

title: P1 exercise — Explain the structure
section: 4. Pressure is not the entire growth mechanism
text:
4. Pressure is not the entire growth mechanism
A cell rapidly takes up water but does not undergo irreversible expansion. Offer two compatible explanations involving the wall or growth state. What observation would distinguish temporary swelling from lasting growth? Explain why wall loosening and synthesis must be coordinated.

title: P1 exercise — Explain the structure
text:
5. Three genomes, one cell
An invented mutation changes a nuclear gene encoding a protein imported into chloroplasts. The chloroplast DNA sequence is unchanged, but photosynthetic performance decreases. Is this contradictory? Explain protein location versus gene location. Then explain how two tissues sharing a nuclear genome can have different organelles and functions without invoking different DNA sequences.

title: P1 exercise — Explain the structure
text:
Completion check
Your answers should distinguish tissues from organs, membranes from walls, division from expansion and gene location from protein destination. Return to the self-check after revising one explanation from discussion.

title: P1 — Building a plant
text:
How does a seedling function?
Obtain resources, transport material, support growth.
Explain the connection from cell feature to whole-plant function.

title: P1 — Building a plant
text:
A cell has several boundaries

Plasma membrane: selective exchange
Wall: extracellular mechanics and connections
Tonoplast: vacuolar boundary

title: P1 — Building a plant
text:
Vacuole and turgor
Solutes and water contribute to pressure against a resisting wall.
Wilting can change mechanics before cells die.

title: P1 — Building a plant
text:
Plastids and mitochondria
Chloroplasts support photosynthesis; other plastids have other roles.
Green cells also respire.

title: P1 — Building a plant
text:
Expansion needs coordination
Turgor supplies force.
Wall yielding, synthesis and membrane addition permit lasting expansion.

title: P1 — Building a plant
text:
Two routes
Apoplast: walls and extracellular spaces.
Symplast: connected cytoplasm. Membrane crossing changes the route.

title: P1 — Building a plant
text:
Three tissue systems

Dermal: protection and exchange
Ground: photosynthesis, storage, support
Vascular: transport and support

title: P1 — Building a plant
text:
Xylem and phloem differ
Conducting xylem elements are dead at maturity.
Sieve tubes remain living; companion cells support them. Whole xylem also contains living cells.

title: P1 — Building a plant
text:
Where does growth occur?
Apical meristems contribute length.
Lateral meristems contribute thickening where present.

title: P1 — Building a plant
text:
More cells or longer cells?
100 × 40 µm = 4 mm.
100 × 70 µm = 7 mm; 175 × 40 µm also = 7 mm.
Length alone does not identify the mechanism.

title: P1 — Building a plant
text:
Three genomes cooperate
Nuclear, plastid and mitochondrial expression support one cell.
A protein destination does not identify its gene location.

title: P1 — Building a plant
text:
Explain before naming
Trace CO2, water and exported carbohydrate through a leaf.
Use the tutorial, exercise and self-check.

title: P5 exercise — Evaluate a physiological intervention
text: Use the tutorial. Allow 60–75 minutes, including a short group discussion. All evidence records and numeric trial results below are invented for this exercise. They are not copied from a database or a published study. No transformation, culture or release activity is requested.

title: P5 exercise — Evaluate a physiological intervention
text:
1. Explain survival versus performance
A fictional line closes stomata earlier during drying. It retains more leaf water but makes fewer seeds under one drought regime. Draw a mechanism linking the intervention to both observations. What additional measurements would test the carbon-gain and leaf-temperature explanations? Could the same response be beneficial under a more severe regime? Define the outcome before saying “better”.

title: P5 exercise — Evaluate a physiological intervention
text:
2. Separate annotation from evidence
Use this offline record; an optional comparison with a real TAIR entry can be made if access is available.







Field
Fictional record




Identifier
TEACH-GC1 (invented; not a TAIR locus)


Annotation
Candidate membrane transport regulator


Expression
Reporter detected mainly in guard cells under tested conditions


Perturbation
One transformed line has earlier closure


Similarity
Related sequence in another species has an annotated transport role



Rank the claims: observed reporter location; proven native-protein location; proven causal control of closure; plausible mechanistic hypothesis. Which evidence is direct and which is inferred? Explain why searching a gene name and copying the first description would lose essential uncertainty.

title: P5 exercise — Evaluate a physiological intervention
section: 3. Design controls before interpreting a transformed line
text:
3. Design controls before interpreting a transformed line
The line in task 2 was regenerated through tissue culture. Propose appropriate background and culture controls, multiple independent events and a way to test association with the intended change. Explain what a tissue-specific promoter is intended to achieve and why its specificity needs measurement. Distinguish stable transformation, transient expression and editing.

text:
4. Read a small factorial comparison
The following invented means are seeds per plant from equally sized groups; variation and replication details have deliberately not been supplied.



Line
No herbivores
Herbivores present




Control
100
50


Defence-enhanced

Calculate the line difference in each environment. Explain how the pattern could reflect a defence cost and protection benefit. List the missing design and uncertainty information needed before recommending the line. Do not infer statistical significance from four means.






Direction check





Enhanced minus control is −15 seeds without herbivores and +25 with herbivores. The pattern is condition-dependent. It does not establish the molecular mechanism, the long-term field effect or significance.

title: P5 exercise — Evaluate a physiological intervention
text:
5. Write a reasoned recommendation
Choose either fictional intervention and write 250–350 words addressing its mechanism, intended setting, evidence, limitations and next measurement. Include one potential benefit, one context-specific ecological concern and one question of access or decision power. Identify at least one empirical question and one value judgement. Compare with a stated alternative rather than an unspecified “natural” plant. A recommendation to collect more evidence is valid if you name the evidence and explain how it would affect the decision.

title: P5 exercise — Evaluate a physiological intervention
text:
Completion check
Keep physiological, empirical and ethical reasoning connected. A label such as “GM”, “natural” or “stress-tolerant” does not supply a complete evaluation. Finish with the self-check.

title: P5 — Stress and applications
text:
What does “better” mean?
Survival, carbon gain, biomass and viable seeds are distinct outcomes.
State the intended environment and comparator.

title: P5 — Stress and applications
text:
Exposure to performance
External challenge → response → possible damage/acclimation → longer-term outcome.
Acclimation is not evolutionary adaptation.

title: P5 — Stress and applications
text:
Abiotic stresses differ
Drought, salinity, heat and freezing share some responses but pose different problems.
Salt adds possible ion toxicity to osmotic stress.

title: P5 — Stress and applications
text:
Defence has several layers
Pre-existing barriers and chemicals; local and systemic induced responses.
Hormone pathways interact; attacker context matters.

title: P5 — Stress and applications
text:
Natural products have context
Dose, compartment, exposure and target determine effect.
“Natural” does not establish harmlessness.

title: P5 — Stress and applications
text:
Growth and defence
Costs and protection benefits depend on conditions.
Primary JAZ study provides a specific mechanistic case.

title: P5 — Stress and applications
text:
Models and databases
Record species, stable identifier, evidence and source.
Annotation or expression is not automatically causal proof.

title: P5 — Stress and applications
text:
Transformation differs from regeneration
Delivery, stable/transient outcomes and editing are distinct.
Culture response varies by genotype and tissue.

title: P5 — Stress and applications
text:
Controls protect interpretation
Background and culture controls; multiple independent events; association/complementation where appropriate.
One line is insufficient.

title: P5 — Stress and applications
text:
Tissue-specific expression
A promoter can target expression in place/time. Verify specificity.
Check CO2 uptake, temperature and yield alongside water retention.

title: P5 — Stress and applications
text:
A chemical detector concept
Responsive promoter + reporter may indicate exposure.
Test specificity, calibration, timing, background and plant condition.

title: P5 — Stress and applications
text:
Evidence and ethics
Separate empirical questions from value judgements; consider benefits, costs and decision power.
Apply to the exercise and self-check.

title: P2 exercise — Account for water movement
section: 3. What did the pot actually lose?
text:
3. What did the pot actually lose?
Four individually treated pots lose 24, 27, 22 and 25 g over four hours. Their leaf areas are 0.10, 0.12, 0.10 and 0.11 m². Unplanted soil controls under the same conditions lose a mean of 4 g per pot. For a teaching estimate, subtract 4 g from each loss, then divide by time and leaf area.

Water access depends on potential, pathways and regulation.

−0.2 MPa is higher than −0.8 MPa.

Apoplast, symplast and transmembrane movement.
The endodermal barrier restricts an unrestricted wall-space route into the stele.

CO2 access and vapour loss share a pathway.

Drought responses include channel regulation and later changes.
A hormone is not a physical pore plug.

Essential minerals
Required amounts differ from importance.
Symptoms depend on mobility, age, roots, pH and other stresses.

Pot mass loss = soil evaporation + plant water loss + other changes.
Controls and units determine interpretation.

title: Practical: evidence for tissue identity and function
text:
What observations justify naming a tissue, and how does that tissue help an organ work? Work in pairs for 75–90 minutes, then submit one individual observation sheet. You need paper and a pencil; the cases below supply textual observations. They are deliberately constructed descriptions, not microscope images or records of actual specimens. This activity practises reasoning before a specimen session; passing it does not establish visual identification or dissection skill. A reproducible observation record
For each case record: the features explicitly supplied; the most defensible tissue class; two features supporting it; a likely function; one plausible alternative; and an observation that would discriminate between the two. Keep observation separate from inference. “Several layers of cells” is an observation; “protects against abrasion” is a functional interpretation. Do not infer a named organ from a common epithelial shape alone.

Station 1: interfaces
Case A: a continuous lining appears one cell thick. Cells are flattened, and nuclei interrupt an otherwise thin barrier. A capillary is immediately adjacent; no thick keratin layer is described.
Case B: a lining contains several cell layers. Surface cells are flattened. Deeper cells appear less flattened. The tissue borders a surface exposed to friction.
Case C: a tubular profile has a single layer of approximately cube-shaped cells around a lumen. Nuclei are central. Other sections show many similar tubules, but no specialised border can be resolved.

Classify the epithelia by layer number and surface-cell shape.
Explain why A is compatible with exchange and B with protection. Do not claim every thin lining has the same transport properties.
Could C establish “kidney” on its own? Name an additional contextual feature you would ask to inspect.







Hint





“Simple” and “stratified” describe layers; “squamous”, “cuboidal” and “columnar” describe cell shape. Function also depends on junctions, membrane proteins and the surrounding structures.





Station 2: force and information
Case D: long parallel fibres show repeated transverse bands. Multiple nuclei lie near fibre edges; fibres are not described as branching.
Case E: short branching fibres show transverse bands and central nuclei. Distinct cell-to-cell junction regions are visible.
Case F: spindle-shaped cells each have a central nucleus. No transverse bands are visible; bundles surround a hollow organ.
Case G: large cell bodies contain prominent nuclei and several processes; many smaller supporting cells surround them. The description alone does not specify which processes are axons or dendrites.

Identify the best broad tissue interpretation for each case, explaining the features rather than matching a keyword.
Which two cases are striated? Why is “striated means skeletal” insufficient?
Predict consequences of disrupting coordinated contraction in E and sustained contraction in F. Link the prediction to organ function, not diagnosis of a disease.



Station 3: organ architecture
Sketch a cross-section of a generic transport tube with an inner lining, connective support and a muscular layer. Label the lumen and identify which side contacts the transported material. Explain how a change in muscular diameter can alter flow. Then explain why a tube described this way cannot be identified confidently as either a blood vessel or a gut segment without further observations.
Draw a fish gill lamella and a mammalian alveolar interface as conceptual diagrams, not replicas of slides. Mark the environmental medium, a thin exchange barrier and blood. Write two common exchange requirements and one important difference in ventilation or medium. A functional resemblance does not establish the same evolutionary origin of every component.

title: Practical: evidence for tissue identity and function
section: Turning descriptions into genuine visual practice
text:
Turning descriptions into genuine visual practice
Use the institution’s provided normal-tissue slides when available. For each unknown, begin at low magnification, orient the tissue, then inspect selected features at higher magnification under the local microscope instructions. Record image/slide ID, magnification or scale bar, orientation and two diagnostic observations. Distinguish sectioning angle from biological shape: a longitudinal tube and its cross-section can look very different.
Do not invent a scale or copy an atlas label onto an uncertain feature. Return to the specimen if two alternatives fit. A descriptive record with justified uncertainty is better evidence than a confident name without observations.

title: Practical: evidence for tissue identity and function
text:
Completion check
Leave with the seven case records, two conceptual exchange diagrams and a paragraph answering: “What extra evidence would I need before identifying an unknown organ?” End by naming the visual skill this text exercise cannot verify. Review representative tissue images through the linked learning resources or the course atlas; no image-reuse rights are implied here.






Self-check





A: simple squamous; B: stratified squamous; C: simple cuboidal. D: skeletal muscle; E: cardiac muscle; F: smooth muscle; G: nervous tissue. C’s shape alone cannot establish a kidney origin. The diagrams should show thin barriers and large exchange area, while distinguishing water passing gills from air ventilating lungs. These answers do not replace visual specimen assessment.

title: Practical: growth under reduced watering
text:
Do supplied height measurements support a difference in growth between watering treatments, and what physiological explanations remain possible? This 90-minute practical uses simulated growth data with the data dictionary. It can be completed with paper and a calculator. These are invented observations, not evidence about an actual species, watering recommendation or live experiment.
Twelve plants in separate pots were allocated randomly, six per treatment, after baseline height measurement. Watering is applied individually; pots are interspersed in a common growth space with positions balanced. The same plant is measured seven days later. Assume the defined treatments are the intended difference; real experiments would need records of watering doses, soil moisture, environment, handling and compliance.

title: Practical: growth under reduced watering
section: Growth is a change, not a final size
text:
Growth is a change, not a final size
Calculate height increment as final minus initial height, in mm. A taller plant at the end may have started taller; that is why baseline measurements matter. Here the table permits a within-plant change, followed by a comparison of those changes between independent treatment groups. It is not a paired comparison between a watered plant and an unrelated reduced-water plant.
G01 changes from 30 to 48 mm, an 18 mm increment over seven days. Its average height-increment rate is \(18/7=2.57\) mm day⁻¹. This average is not proof of constant daily growth: two observations cannot reveal a detailed growth trajectory.

title: Practical: growth under reduced watering
text:
Analysis tasks

Check the identifiers, group counts and measurement units. Count the independent pots. Explain why the baseline and final readings do not double that count.
Calculate each plant’s increment and mean daily rate. Check G07 explicitly.
Plot the individual increments by group and calculate group means and ranges. Describe the difference as reduced-water minus watered.
Calculate the relative reduction compared with the watered mean. Explain the difference between a reduction of 8 mm and a reduction of 40%.
Write a short interpretation using the terms observation, explanation and limitation accurately. No significance test is required.







Hint





G07 starts at 31 mm and ends at 41 mm, giving 10 mm rather than 41 mm growth. The denominator for relative reduction is the reference group’s mean increment, not its final mean height.

title: Practical: growth under reduced watering
section: Mechanisms: what could connect water supply to height?
text:
Mechanisms: what could connect water supply to height?
Plant expansion depends on cell-wall properties and water relations; cell production and developmental allocation also influence organ growth. Reduced water availability may alter turgor, stomatal conductance, carbon acquisition and hormonal signalling. These are candidate connections to the observed response, not mechanisms established by measuring height alone.

Draw two distinct causal pathways from reduced watering to lower height increment: one involving cell expansion/water status and one involving gas exchange or carbon supply. Mark which variables this dataset actually measures and which would need new observations.
A student says “shorter plants have less auxin, so the hormone caused this”. Explain the unsupported steps. How could hormone sensitivity or spatial distribution complicate an interpretation based on one hormone measurement?
Propose one non-destructive follow-up observation for each pathway and state what result would be consistent with it. A consistent result is not necessarily exclusive evidence; name an alternative explanation.

title: Practical: growth under reduced watering
section: Development and stress must be distinguished
text:
Development and stress must be distinguished
Plants may alter allocation, leaf area, root growth or the timing of development under changed conditions. A lower height increment is not always equivalent to lower total biomass, lower survival or a failed adaptation. Conversely, surviving while ceasing growth does not establish that a crop maintains yield. The outcome used to define “tolerance” must be explicit.
Design a follow-up comparison of two hypothetical genotypes under watered and reduced-water conditions. Draw the four genotype × treatment groups. Specify independent pots, allocation across positions, a relevant outcome and the same measurement time. Do not place all genotype 1 plants in one cabinet and genotype 2 plants in another. Keep the treatment contrast available within each genotype and the genotype contrast within each treatment.

title: Practical: growth under reduced watering
text:
Reporting and completion check
Submit the increment table, observation plot, mean comparison, two mechanism diagrams and a follow-up design. In the discussion distinguish the strong claim supported by this constructed example—different height increments under its stipulated conditions—from broader untested claims about drought resistance, carbon balance, hormones or field performance.






Numerical check





Watered increments are 18, 20, 22, 19, 21 and 20 mm, mean 20 and range 18–22. Reduced-water increments are 10, 12, 14, 11, 13 and 12 mm, mean 12 and range 10–14. Reduced-water minus watered is −8 mm; the relative reduction is 40%. Mean daily rates are about 2.86 and 1.71 mm day⁻¹. The constructed table has six independent pots per treatment.



Continue to scientific reporting or return to the practical route.

This activity connects anatomy, water relations, photosynthesis, genetics and ethics. It does not ask for a general vote for or against all genetically modified plants. Prepare independently for 60 minutes, discuss in a group for 45 minutes, then give a short individual presentation.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
text:
Sources to read
Use the original article by Karavolias and colleagues (2023), “Paralog editing tunes rice stomatal density to maintain photosynthesis and improve drought tolerance,” Plant Physiology 192, 1168–1182, DOI 10.1093/plphys/kiad183. The open full text includes methods, figures and limitations. The PubMed record gives bibliographic details. Read the abstract and introduction, then focus on stomatal density, gas exchange and water conservation. Inspect figure legends and relevant methods; do not rely on the abstract alone.
For broader context use National Academies (2016), Genetically Engineered Crops: Experiences and Prospects, summary. This is an evidence synthesis, not a second primary experiment. It supports discussion of different kinds of evidence and societal questions. It is not a statement of current local law; regulatory decisions require current official information and are outside this exercise.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
text:
Vocabulary bridge
A paralog is a member of a gene family arising through duplication. Related genes need not have identical expression or effects. A knockout disrupts gene function. Stomatal density counts stomata per surface area; stomatal aperture describes individual pore openings. Both can affect conductance, so fewer stomata do not automatically predict a proportional fall in measured gas exchange.
The research compares edited rice lines with a reference background, using anatomical and physiological measurements. Connect a developmental change with functional evidence while checking trade-offs and experimental scope. Do not assume a greenhouse result establishes performance in every farming environment.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
text:
Individual evidence sheet
Choose one figure comparing gas exchange and one comparing water conservation or performance. Record actual figure/panel identifiers from the article. For each, answer in your own words:

What question does this comparison address, and what is the outcome variable?
Which lines/conditions are compared? What reference is appropriate?
What do the axes and units mean? What does one point represent?
How does the caption define sample size and error bars? Does a repeated measurement create a new independent plant?
What pattern is supported? Use a numerical value only if its source and precision are clear; do not guess exact values from a small image.
Which proposed mechanism is directly measured, and which is inferred?
What would challenge an overly broad claim that fewer stomata always improve performance?

Trace one result to its methods. Record whether measurements were made in a greenhouse, chamber or field and whether the same conditions apply to every result. If a detail cannot be located, say so and identify where you looked. Resolve uncertainty rather than inventing a number.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
section: Group discussion: three kinds of question
text:
Group discussion: three kinds of question
Physiological: Can a developmental manipulation conserve water while maintaining gas exchange under the conditions tested? Explain a mechanism and possible trade-offs involving cooling, carbon supply or changing light.
Evidential: What tests are needed for a different cultivar, soil, climate, drought regime or field setting? Water conservation is not automatically a yield benefit. Describe one follow-up comparison with a relevant reference, independent units and a clear outcome.
Ethical and societal: Who might benefit, bear costs or make decisions? Consider access to seed, affordability, farmer choice, local priorities, environmental effects and alternatives such as breeding or management. Distinguish empirical claims needing data from value judgments about what should be prioritised. A possible benefit does not erase a possible risk; a possible risk does not establish that it occurs.
Each group writes a decision scenario with an explicit context—for example, a proposed locally evaluated drought-response cultivar—and lists the evidence it would request. Do not claim the article proves a particular product is currently approved or commercially available.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
text:
Individual presentation
Prepare a five-minute presentation plus two minutes of questions. This timing is a teaching suggestion, not a formal examination rule. Use up to five slides or an equivalent spoken explanation:

The physiological problem and the stomatal trade-off.
The developmental intervention and comparison design.
One anatomical finding and one physiological result.
Limits, an alternative explanation or a needed follow-up.
A conclusion separating evidence from ethical priorities.

Cite the original article and synthesis. If showing a figure, check its licence and attribution requirements; a reference alone is not permission to reuse every element. Alternatively, draw your own conceptual diagram and describe findings orally. Questions should probe reasoning, not demand memorisation of every molecular detail.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
text:
Feedback and completion
Listeners record one well-supported claim, one scope limit and one question. Then write a 150-word revision explaining how feedback clarifies your conclusion. Keep the evidence sheet, sources, presentation and revision. Feedback should address reasoning, source use and physiological accuracy, not require a preferred political position.
Return to the practical route.

title: Practical: water loss, leaf area and a mass balance
text:
How does moving air relate to water loss from a hypothetical plant setup? This 90-minute classroom practical uses the plant-water CSV and data dictionary. No plant manipulation or apparatus procedure is required. Use the course’s actual laboratory protocol for any future measurements.
Eight independently potted plants are randomised to still or moving air, four per group. Each pot receives its setting independently; temperature, humidity, illumination and position are controlled or balanced. Soil surfaces are covered. Matched plant-free covered setups lose 0.10 g during the interval. Assume that background applies to each experimental setup. These are supplied simplifications, not observations you should claim to have verified.

title: Practical: water loss, leaf area and a mass balance
section: From a balance reading to a physiological quantity
text:
From a balance reading to a physiological quantity
An initial-to-final mass difference is a whole-setup measurement. In this exercise we attribute corrected mass loss primarily to transpired water. This is an approximation: real mass balances also require attention to leaks, soil evaporation, material added/removed and other fluxes. A balance does not measure a stomatal aperture or distinguish stomatal from cuticular water loss.
Calculate:
\[
\Delta m_{corrected}=m_{initial}-m_{final}-\Delta m_{blank}
\]
\[
E_{area}=\frac{1000\,\Delta m_{corrected}}{A\,(t/60)}.
\]
The mass values are in g, \(A\) is the stated one-sided leaf area in cm², and \(t\) is in min. The result is mg cm⁻² h⁻¹. One-sided area is a measurement convention; state it consistently rather than switching to two-sided area midway through a comparison.

Worked check
W01 loses 0.80 g. After a 0.10 g background correction, 0.70 g = 700 mg is attributed to the plant. Its area is 50 cm² and the interval 0.5 h. The area-specific loss is \(700/(50\times0.5)=28\) mg cm⁻² h⁻¹. The correction is subtracted once per setup, not once per leaf.

title: Practical: water loss, leaf area and a mass balance
text:
Tasks

Identify the experimental unit, allocation groups and number of independent replicates. Why would one shared still-air cabinet and one shared moving-air cabinet weaken a treatment comparison?
Calculate corrected water loss and area-specific rate for all eight pots. Check W06 by hand before summarising the groups.
Draw an observation plot and calculate group means. Describe the size and variation of the difference in the given units.
Draw the path from soil water through root, xylem, leaf air spaces and stomata to the atmosphere. Mark where vapour diffusion occurs.
Explain how moving air can change the boundary layer at the leaf surface. Why might stomatal regulation prevent a simple proportional response to wind speed in a real plant?
Decide whether the data establish stomatal opening, photosynthetic rate or a species’ drought tolerance. Explain what further measurements each claim would need.







Hint





W06’s observed 2.0 g loss becomes 1.9 g after correction, then 1900 mg. Divide by 25 cm² h, not by 1500 cm² min while labelling the answer per hour.

title: Practical: water loss, leaf area and a mass balance
section: Water potential: use the sign, not just the magnitude
text:
Water potential: use the sign, not just the magnitude
For a short cell-level comparison neglect gravity and matric components and use \(\Psi_w=\Psi_s+\Psi_p\). A cell has solute potential −0.8 MPa and pressure potential +0.3 MPa, so its water potential is −0.5 MPa. The adjacent solution has water potential −0.2 MPa. Predict the initial direction of net water movement across a permeable membrane, assuming the relevant solutes do not freely cross. Explain why the movement slows as cell state changes.
Then consider an adjacent solution at −0.9 MPa. The direction reverses: water moves from the higher water potential (less negative value) toward the lower water potential. The two cases do not allow you to compute a flux without hydraulic conductance, area and other information. Do not equate a potential difference in MPa with a mass-loss rate.

title: Practical: water loss, leaf area and a mass balance
text:
Completion check
Submit a labelled water-path diagram, a worked W06 calculation, the eight rates and group means, and an interpretation linking gas exchange and water conservation. Include one design limitation and your water-potential predictions.






Self-check





Still-air rates: 28, 36, 44 and 36 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹; moving-air rates: 60, 76, 92 and 76. Means are 36 and 76, a difference of 40. The cell in −0.2 MPa solution initially gains water; in −0.9 MPa solution it loses water. More water loss alone does not establish greater carbon gain or drought tolerance.



For background, read the water-potential and transpiration sections in OpenStax: transport of water and solutes. Return to the practical route.

A repeatable weekly rhythm
Begin with the biological question and a short prerequisite check. Read the tutorial in sections, using the slides for discussion and the exercise for application. Complete the practical activity alongside the relevant mechanism, then revisit the quiz after a delay. Reserve time for reading, observation, writing and feedback rather than treating every topic as another lecture.

text:
Review without adding methods
At the end of each half, attempt the corresponding revision tasks without the solutions visible. Reopen the unit where your mechanism is weak. A labelled diagram, a small calculation and a clear explanation usually reveal more than repeatedly rereading a list of terms. There is no extra computing week.
